::: {#thm-sum-rule}
#### Sums of big-O functions

Let $f$, $g$ and $h$ be functions (@def-function) from the natural numbers (@def-natural-numbers) to the real numbers (@def-real-numbers).
If $f(n) = O(h(n))$ and $g(n) = O(h(n))$ (@def-big-o), then $f(n) + g(n) = O(h(n))$.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

Let $c_1$, $N_1$ be witnesses (@def-witness) for $f(n) = O(h(n))$,
and $c_2$, $N_2$ witnesses for $g(n) = O(h(n))$.
Let $N$ be the larger of $N_1$ and $N_2$.
The triangle inequality [@wikipedia_triangle_inequality] says that $\abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}$ for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.
For every natural number $n \ge N$, both $n \ge N_1$ and $n \ge N_2$ hold, so

$$
\ba
\abs{f(n) + g(n)}
&\le \abs{f(n)} + \abs{g(n)}
&& \text{(triangle inequality)}
\\&\le c_1 \abs{h(n)} + c_2 \abs{h(n)}
&& \text{(} n \ge N_1 \text{ and } n \ge N_2 \text{)}
\\&= (c_1 + c_2) \abs{h(n)}.
\ea
$$

So $c_1 + c_2$ and $N$ are witnesses for $f(n) + g(n) = O(h(n))$.

:::

:::
